records.sourceFile: Clinically feasible dual-task detects residual post-concussion deficits after return-to-play.pdf

paper.citation: Hashida K, Shirahata K, Furutani T, Tamura K. Clinically feasible dual-task detects residual post-concussion deficits after return-to-play. Journal of Sports Sciences. 2024.
paper.abstract: A prospective cohort study compared a clinically feasible dual-task test (Expanded Timed Get Up and Go with an auditory odd-or-even task) with single-task performance in adolescent athletes with concussion and matched controls. The concussion group was tested 7 to 10 days after injury and again after completing a graduated return-to-play protocol.
paper.tldr: After athletes were cleared to return to play, those with concussion were still slower than matched controls on the dual-task walk test, by about 5.7 seconds on average. Symptom checklists showed no group difference at that point, so this test may detect deficits that standard checks miss.
paper.methods: Concussion and control groups each had 10 male and 10 female participants, matched by age, sex and sport. Each participant completed two single tasks (ETGUG and an auditory odd-or-even switch task) in randomized order, then the two combined as a dual task, with symptoms recorded before and after each session. Group, task and time effects were analysed with mixed-design ANOVAs and post-hoc tests.
paper.findings: At 7 to 10 days, the concussion group was slower than controls on single-task ETGUG (2.61 s, p = 0.018) and dual-task ETGUG (3.49 s, p = 0.014). At return to play, the concussion group remained slower on single-task (2.85 s, p = 0.007) and dual-task (5.65 s, p < 0.001) ETGUG, the task-by-group interaction was significant, and only the concussion group still showed a significant dual-task cost (4.46 s, p = 0.008). Controls got faster between sessions on both tasks, while the concussion group did not, and symptom totals did not differ between groups at return to play.
paper.limitations: The sample is small (20 per group), drawn from high school and university athletes at more than one test site, and the gap between the two sessions varied by person and was not controlled. The text and tables disagree slightly: the RTP task-by-group interaction is p < 0.001 in the text and p = 0.001 in Table 2, and the 95% CI for the RTP dual-task difference is 2.56 to 8.74 s in the text and 2.53 to 8.78 s in Table 3. The paper reports no reliability data in this population and did not test the deficits against later outcomes.
paper.practicalImplications: The test needs only a chair, a cone set 10 m away, a phone timer and someone to call random numbers, so it can be run in an athletic training room. Because the paper leaves open whether baseline data are needed, an individual athlete's time should not be read against a norm without a local baseline or control comparison.
paper.athleteDev: For performance staff, the test measures how well divided attention holds up while walking. The paper does not link dual-task speed to training load, readiness or performance output, so it cannot guide training prescription.
paper.rtp: The authors recommend adding a dual-task walk-and-count test to concussion assessment, because athletes cleared to return still performed slower than matched controls as a group. The study does not show that the test should change individual clearance decisions, gives no cut-off, and does not test whether these deficits predict re-injury.

records.sourceFile: Comparing the maximal horizontal deceleration demands between a novel acceleration to deceleration assessment and the 505 change of direction test.pdf

paper.citation: Philipp NM, Scott AA, Caldwell BR, Cabarkapa D, Johnson QR, Fry AC. Comparing the maximal horizontal deceleration demands between a novel acceleration to deceleration assessment and the 505 change of direction test. Journal of Human Sport and Exercise. 2024;19(3):803-814.
paper.abstract: Laboratory comparison of 19 recreationally trained, college-aged athletes performing a 10-m acceleration-to-deceleration assessment (ADA) and the 505 change of direction test, measured with an inertial measurement unit system. Six of 12 deceleration metrics differed between tests, with the 505 showing greater average deceleration and braking force, and the ADA showing shorter stopping time and distance, although these two stopping measures had insufficient reliability.
paper.tldr: In 19 recreationally trained athletes, the 505 test produced greater average deceleration, braking force, stopping time and stopping distance than a 10-m acceleration-to-deceleration task with a cued braking point and no fixed stopping point. Stopping time and distance were not reliable enough to track small changes, so the two tests should be treated as measuring different braking demands rather than as interchangeable.
paper.methods: Within-session comparison of ADA (three trials) and 505 (four trials, two per leg) using an Xsens MVN Awinda IMU suit sampling at 100 Hz, with metrics processed in Athlete Analytics. Between-test differences were tested with paired t-tests and Hedges' g, and reliability was assessed with ICC (2,k), SEM and minimal difference across trials.
paper.findings: Average approach velocity and momentum did not differ between tests. The 505 showed greater average deceleration (4.10 vs 3.32 m/s2, ES -2.46) and braking force (313.6 vs 252.4 N, ES -1.61), longer stopping time (1.41 vs 1.20 s) and distance (5.38 vs 4.17 m), shorter brake-step contact time (0.18 vs 0.20 s) and brake steps placed closer to the centre of mass (36.1 vs 41.0 cm). Stopping time and distance ICCs were 0.51 and 0.56 for stopping time and 0.13 and 0.26 for stopping distance, with the authors describing these as insufficient.
paper.limitations: The authors acknowledge that the sample had little prior experience with either test, which may inflate variability, and that deceleration phase COM drop had high SEM. The reliability of average deceleration was poor (ICC 0.34 for ADA and 0.47 for 505), and the Table 3 confidence interval for average deceleration (-0.91; 0.78) and ES interval (-3.33; 1.88) are not internally consistent with the reported means. The SEM is described as coming from an ANOVA across three trials although the 505 had four, and the abstract's 'reductions in velocity' is not a separately reported metric.
paper.practicalImplications: When deceleration is quantified with IMUs, these results suggest that a 505 test with a fixed turn point and an ADA with a cued braking point but no fixed stopping point should not be treated as interchangeable, since braking force and stopping metrics differ. Because stopping time and distance were unreliable, staff should check the minimal difference values (for example 2.48 m for ADA stopping distance) before treating a change in these measures as real.
paper.athleteDev: The paper suggests the predetermined turn in the 505 imposes a different braking demand from the ADA, with longer stopping time and distance, greater braking force and shorter brake-step contacts. The authors speculate that this demands different neuromuscular and skill qualities, but the study did not measure performance outcomes, so its use for training selection remains an inference.
paper.rtp: The study tested healthy recreationally trained athletes and did not assess injury, rehabilitation or return-to-sport status, so it cannot be used to clear an athlete or set return-to-play benchmarks. The minimal-difference values reported, such as about 2.5 m for ADA stopping distance, suggest these metrics would miss small changes in braking capacity during rehabilitation.

records.sourceFile: Concussion injuries in sports and the role of instrumented mouthguards - A mini review.pdf

paper.citation: Chilmeran Z, Akhtar MU, Sharafeldin A-BK, Gaynor D. Concussion injuries in sports and the role of instrumented mouthguards: a mini review. Frontiers in Bioengineering and Biotechnology. 2025;13:1567429.
paper.abstract: This mini review summarises concussion in contact sports, including mechanisms, prevalence and long-term effects, and examines the validity of instrumented mouthguards (iMGs) for measuring head impacts. The authors report that iMGs can measure linear and rotational acceleration with low error in several studies, but that accuracy depends on fit, sensor coupling and signal filtering. Citing a consensus statement, they describe iMGs as research tools that need further refinement and standardised validation before reliable clinical or field use.
paper.tldr: Instrumented mouthguards measure head impacts with reasonable accuracy in some validation studies, but fit and sensor coupling strongly affect their readings. The review states that they are still research tools and cannot diagnose concussion on their own.
paper.methods: Narrative mini review. The paper does not describe a systematic search or study selection criteria. It draws on prior work on concussion epidemiology and pathophysiology, mouthguard history, and iMG validation in headform, cadaveric, laboratory and field studies.
paper.findings: The review cites an observational NFL study (1,302 concussions in 1,004 players, 2015 to 2019) and an NHL rate of about 5.8 to 6.1 concussions per 100 games. One high school football comparison of an iMG with the helmet-mounted HIT System (133 paired events) found low average error but significant variability in higher-impact events, and one headform study reported mean absolute errors as low as 7%. In 915 female youth soccer players, an iMG had 69.2% sensitivity and 80.3% positive predictive value, which the authors describe as confirming reliability for on-field use, while they also report that iMGs lack validity at high impact velocities and that fit, direct contact and filter cutoffs affect accuracy.
paper.limitations: The review does not describe how the cited studies were selected, so the evidence is not systematically weighed. It notes that female and younger athletes are under-represented in iMG research and that validation and calibration protocols are not standardised. The authors also state that evidence on whether mouthguards reduce concussion is inconsistent and unclear.
paper.practicalImplications: Before using iMGs, staff should check whether a device has been validated in their sport and age group, and should check fit and sensor coupling before trusting readings. The review advises that iMG data alone should not diagnose concussion, and that clinical assessment with SCAT-6 and expert judgement remain essential.
paper.athleteDev: For performance staff, iMGs can record head impacts in real time, so they can support monitoring of impact exposure. The readings are sensitive to fit and comfort, and the review notes barriers to adoption, so the data should be treated as one monitoring signal. The review does not evaluate training load or performance outcomes.
paper.rtp: The review does not study return to play and gives no return-to-play criteria. Its statement that iMG data alone cannot diagnose concussion, and that clinical assessment is still needed, means impact readings should not be used to clear an athlete to return.

records.sourceFile: Consensus Head Acceleration Measurement Practices (CHAMP) - Origins, methods, transparency and disclose.pdf

paper.citation: Arbogast KB, Caccese JB, Buckley TA, et al. Consensus Head Acceleration Measurement Practices (CHAMP): Origins, Methods, Transparency and Disclosure. Annals of Biomedical Engineering. 2022.
paper.abstract: This consensus paper describes the origins and voting methods of the Consensus Head Acceleration Measurement Practices (CHAMP) group. It introduces reporting checklists for head kinematic measurement studies and for disclosing industry involvement.
paper.tldr: Use the CHAMP 2022 checklists to report how a head-acceleration device was validated, verified, windowed and processed. Disclose sponsor and industry involvement so readers can judge bias.
paper.methods: Expert working groups drafted best-practice chapters in six areas. Statements were voted on at a March 2022 consensus conference, with 80% agreement required for acceptance. The authors then built reporting checklists aligned with five methods and a disclosure table.
paper.findings: At least 80% agreement was reached for every statement, often after discussion and revision, so no dissent statements were needed. The checklists list items such as sensor specifications, surrogate and mounting details, event verification, data processing, and reporting of validation metrics and false-positive rates. The paper also lists six types of industry involvement that should be disclosed, including funding, in-kind equipment, proprietary software and help with analysis.
paper.limitations: The paper reports no measured data, so the checklists have not been tested for their effect on study quality. The authors state the checklists are not all-encompassing and will need updating, and not every item has a published example. Financial ties to the NFL and Football Research Inc. are disclosed for several authors, and conference support came from the same organisations.
paper.practicalImplications: When reviewing or planning head-acceleration monitoring, check whether the study reports device validation, event verification, data processing and false-positive or false-negative rates before using its impact counts. Disclosure of sensor-company or league involvement should be read as a transparency requirement, not as proof of bias.
paper.athleteDev: Staff who use head-impact sensors for monitoring should compare players or seasons only when the data are verified and processed in comparable ways. The paper provides reporting and methods guidance and no training-load or performance prescription.
paper.rtp: This paper cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It contains no injury thresholds, clinical criteria or concussion diagnostic standards.

records.sourceFile: Copenhagen five second squeeze a     valid indicator of sports related hip and groin function (1).pdf

paper.citation: Thorborg K, Branci S, Nielsen MP, Langelund MT, Hölmich P. Copenhagen five-second squeeze: a valid indicator of sports-related hip and groin function. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2017;51:594-599.
paper.abstract: This validation study tested a five-second hip-adduction squeeze in 667 subelite male football players, who rated groin pain from 0 to 10 during the squeeze and completed the Copenhagen Hip and Groin Outcome Score (HAGOS). Construct validity, responsiveness, reliability and floor and ceiling effects were assessed.
paper.tldr: The pain score from a five-second squeeze tracks sports-related hip and groin function in football players and was reliable in a small test-retest sample. A pain score of 6 or more indicated substantially impaired function in this study, which the authors suggest should prompt clinical assessment.
paper.methods: Cross-sectional validation study following COSMIN guidance. Construct validity used 667 players at season start, responsiveness and floor and ceiling effects used 52 players tested again later in the season, and test-retest reliability used 10 players with stable status. Analyses used Spearman correlations, Kruskal-Wallis and Mann-Whitney tests, and Lin's concordance correlation coefficient for reliability.
paper.findings: Squeeze pain correlated with lower HAGOS Sport scores at season start (rho -0.61, p<0.01, n=665) and in the 52-player subgroup early and later in the season (rho -0.79 and -0.76), and change scores correlated with HAGOS Sport change scores (rho -0.51). Median HAGOS Sport scores were 97 for pain 0 to 2, 69 for 3 to 5 and 47 for 6 to 10, and test-retest concordance was 0.90 (95% CI 0.67 to 0.97) in 10 players. Only 4 of 39 symptomatic players (10%) scored at the floor or ceiling, below the 15% threshold, so no floor or ceiling effect was declared.
paper.limitations: The reliability sample was 10 players, and reliability analysis included only players whose scores changed by 10 points or less; the responsiveness sample was the 52 players who attended a clinical examination. Change scores correlated more strongly with HAGOS Symptoms (rho -0.64) than with HAGOS Sport, and the subgroup analyses by diagnosis were post hoc, with 24 and 15 players. The authors note that players may under-report pain when they know a high score could stop them playing, and the study did not test whether the cut-offs predict injury or return to play.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff can use the five-second squeeze as a quick, equipment-free pain and function check for football players with groin pain. The authors' traffic-light scheme suggests stopping football and seeking clinical assessment at a pain score of 6 or more, clinical review at 3 to 5, and treating 0 to 2 as few restrictions rather than full clearance.
paper.athleteDev: The paper does not measure performance. Its relevance to performance staff is as a rapid screen of sport-specific hip and groin function, which the authors suggest can inform participation decisions alongside clinical review.
paper.rtp: The authors suggest the traffic-light categories can guide football participation, but say that players with a score of 0 to 2 may still need clinical review before return to play. The study does not test return-to-play outcomes, so it supports screening and monitoring rather than clearance decisions.

records.sourceFile: Development of an Athlete Diet  Index for Rapid Dietary Assessment of Athletes.pdf

paper.citation: Capling L, Gifford JA, Beck KL, Flood VM, Slater GJ, Denyer GS, et al. Development of an Athlete Diet Index for Rapid Dietary Assessment of Athletes. International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism. 2019 (accepted manuscript).
paper.abstract: This study describes the development of an Athlete Diet Index (ADI), an electronic food-based tool for rapid dietary assessment of athletes. Items came from sports nutritionist focus groups, a modified Delphi survey and an athlete pilot. The final 68-item tool was rated easy to use and relevant by pilot athletes, and the authors report content and face validity. Scoring and criterion validation are still needed.
paper.tldr: A 68-item electronic Athlete Diet Index was developed with sports nutritionists and tested with athletes for content and face validity. Pilot athletes found it easy to complete and relevant, but its scoring and accuracy against established dietary methods have not yet been tested.
paper.methods: Mixed-methods study in three phases. Phase 1 used focus groups with 20 accredited sports nutritionists, coded thematically in NVivo. Phase 2 used a modified Delphi survey of 9 of these nutritionists over two rounds. Phase 3 piloted the electronic tool with 15 athletes, who rated comprehension and relevance on 5-point scales, and completion time was recorded.
paper.findings: Focus groups identified athlete-specific features such as training load and injury status, food images and serve sizes, nutrition and hydration around training, meal patterns and supplement use. In the Delphi survey, 6 of 71 draft items were recommended for deletion and minor modifications were suggested for 54, with consensus for inclusion after a second round. The final tool has 68 items: core nutrition (45), performance nutrition (15) and personal information (8); all pilot athletes rated it easy (40%) or very easy (60%) to understand and relevant (37%) or very relevant (63%), and median completion time was 17.5 minutes (range 13 to 26).
paper.limitations: Only content and face validity were tested, with no scoring matrix, no comparison with established dietary methods and no reliability testing. The pilot sample was small, mostly female, and drawn from water polo and rowing. The authors note that the researchers' own sports nutrition experience may have influenced responses.
paper.practicalImplications: Sports nutrition staff could use a brief electronic screen to identify athletes whose intake needs follow-up and to see changes across training phases. The authors advise that it should not replace detailed dietary assessment or individual guidance. Scoring and validation are needed before it is used to judge diet quality.
paper.athleteDev: The tool asks about training load, nutrition and hydration practices around training, and supplement use alongside usual food intake. Without a scoring matrix it cannot yet show whether intake matches training demands, and its items have not been tested against performance outcomes.
paper.rtp: The study addresses dietary assessment in athletes in general, and only one of the 15 pilot athletes was injured. It does not evaluate nutrition for rehabilitation or return to play and cannot be used to set injury nutrition plans.

records.sourceFile: Differences Between Relative and        Absolute Speed and Metabolic Thresholds in Rugby League.pdf

paper.citation: Scott TJ, Thornton HR, Scott MTU, Dascombe BJ, Duthie GM. Differences Between Relative and Absolute Speed and Metabolic Thresholds in Rugby League. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2018;13(3):298-304.
paper.abstract: This study compared relative speed and metabolic thresholds, derived from the 30-15 Intermittent Fitness Test, with absolute thresholds for quantifying match-play running in elite rugby league. Distances above relative thresholds correlated strongly with absolute thresholds, but differences were large by position and fitness. The authors conclude that absolute high-intensity speed thresholds underestimate high-intensity running load for many players.
paper.tldr: Absolute speed thresholds (over 5.2 m/s) underestimate high-intensity running for many rugby league players, especially those with lower fitness. A threshold derived from a 30-15 IFT gives an individual reference that may suit squad monitoring.
paper.methods: GPS match data were collected from 26 professional NRL players across the 2013 season (346 match files). The 30-15 IFT was repeated at four time points about six weeks apart to update individual thresholds. Distances above each threshold were compared using Pearson correlations and magnitude-based effect sizes.
paper.findings: Distance above VT1IFT and MIRTh correlated at r = .94, VT2IFT and HIRTh at r = .94, and HPmetVT2 and HPmetTh at r = .93. Distance above VT2IFT was almost certainly greater than HIRTh for all positional groups (effect size 0.79 to 1.03), with the largest differences in middle forwards and outside backs. Absolute MIRTh over- or underestimated VT1IFT distance depending on position and fitness, and edge forwards covered moderately less distance above HPmetVT2 than HPmetTh.
paper.limitations: Relative thresholds are estimated from the 30-15 IFT, and the authors note that the assumed link between this test and the ventilatory thresholds may vary between individuals. The abstract and results call the 138 to 167% values 'increases', but Table 2 means put VT2IFT distance at about 138 to 169% of HIRTh distance (for example, outside backs 809 m vs 535 m is about 151%, not the 144% reported), and the Practical Applications cite an absolute HIR threshold of over 5.5 m/s while the Methods use over 5.2 m/s. The discussion also describes adjustables and edge forwards as covering 'substantially less' distance above VT1IFT than MIRTh, while the results report most likely the same distances; only one season was observed.
paper.practicalImplications: Squads can set individual high-intensity running references using a 30-15 IFT-based VT2 threshold without laboratory gas analysis. Absolute speed bands are likely to understate high-intensity load for lower-fitness players and to overstate moderate-intensity load for higher-fitness players. Repeat the field test across the season, because the authors changed thresholds when fitness changed.
paper.athleteDev: Use individual relative thresholds when prescribing and monitoring high-intensity running in rugby league. Position-based absolute speed bands can misstate the work of players with different fitness levels. Treat the 30-15 IFT-derived values as estimates, as the authors do.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It describes match-play running in fit professional players and does not assess injured athletes or return-to-play criteria.

records.sourceFile: Dimensionality Reduction for Countermovement Jump Metrics.pdf

paper.citation: James LP, Suppiah H, McGuigan MR, Carey DL. Dimensionality Reduction for Countermovement Jump Metrics. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2021 (ahead of print).
paper.abstract: This brief report applies principal component analysis (PCA) and maximum likelihood factor analysis to countermovement jump (CMJ) variables from three cohorts recorded on three different devices. About 90% of the variance in each data set was explained by 3 or 4 principal components, and 2 to 3 factors explained the jump.
paper.tldr: Applying PCA and factor analysis to three CMJ data sets showed that about 90% of the variance can be captured by 3 or 4 components, so a practitioner can report fewer CMJ variables. The method is demonstrated on three specific samples and devices and does not show which metrics matter most for performance.
paper.methods: Three cohorts were tested on different devices: recreationally trained males (n = 16; force platform, 2000 Hz), competitive mixed martial arts athletes (n = 29; linear position transducer, 100 Hz) and junior elite Australian football players (n = 19; ForceDecks force platform, 1000 Hz). Three trials were performed per set and the best trial was analysed. PCA (singular value decomposition) and maximum likelihood factor analysis with varimax rotation were applied after checking factorability with Bartlett's test and the Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin measure.
paper.findings: Bartlett's test was significant and KMO was acceptable (0.51 to 0.65) for all sets. About 90% of variance was explained by 3 components in set 1 and 4 in sets 2 and 3, and scree plots suggested retaining 2 factors for sets 1 and 2 and possibly 3 to 4 for set 3. The authors note that the factors appeared to group variables into output-type (velocities and displacements), causal (force and impulse) and timing (time to peak) constructs.
paper.limitations: The three samples are small (16 to 29 per set), use different devices and variable lists (Table 1), and the authors state that component contents may vary with population and time of season. The abstract reports over 90% of variance explained, whereas the results section reports about 90%; this record uses the results values. Sex is stated only for set 1, and health status is not stated for any set.
paper.practicalImplications: Practitioners who collect many CMJ variables can run PCA or factor analysis on their own data to find a smaller set that holds most of the variance. Where interpretability matters, select one variable that correlates strongly with each component and prefer the most reliable option, as the authors suggest. Re-check the structure on the staff's own athletes and devices before fixing a variable set.
paper.athleteDev: Use a reduced set of CMJ variables, one from each independent component, to track changes across training blocks. The paper's example choices (average power, average velocity and peak displacement from set 1) are illustrations from one device and sample, not recommendations. Confirm that the retained variables relate to the demands of the sport, since the paper does not test this.
paper.rtp: Not applicable. The study covers variable reduction for CMJ data and includes no injured athletes and no return-to-sport outcome, so it cannot inform return-to-sport decisions.

records.sourceFile: Does the operating tempeature of accelerometers affect data measurement during static and dynamic conditions in sports - A randomized-control trial.pdf

paper.citation: Gómez-Carmona CD, Rojas-Valverde D, Ibáñez SJ, Pino-Ortega J. Does the operating temperature of accelerometers affect data measurement during static and dynamic conditions in sports? A randomized-control trial. Proc Inst Mech Eng Part P J Sports Eng Technol. 2023.
paper.abstract: Two operating temperatures were compared for WIMU PRO inertial devices in a static trial and in a 60-minute U-16 soccer session. Internal temperature and resultant acceleration differed early in the sessions, while PlayerLoad did not differ significantly.
paper.tldr: Accelerometers that had not warmed up to their operating temperature gave different acceleration values early in the session (up to about 30 minutes when static and about 13 minutes during play). PlayerLoad totals were not significantly affected in this study.
paper.methods: Ecological design comparing devices switched on at manufacturer's optimal operating temperature (38-39 C) with devices switched on at session start. Static trial in a docking station and dynamic trial in a 60-minute U-16 small-sided game session with 14 male players wearing paired units in a harness at the interscapular level. Internal temperature, resultant acceleration and PlayerLoad (PLRT) were compared with repeated-measures t-tests in 1-minute averages.
paper.findings: Internal temperature differed between the two temperature conditions for the first 31 minutes in the static trial and the first 20 minutes in the dynamic trial. Resultant acceleration differed for the first 29 minutes (static) and, per the results text, the first 13 minutes (dynamic), mostly with small effects during play. PLRT dynamics and accumulated PLRT did not differ significantly (static p = 0.06, d = 0.19; dynamic p = 0.71, d = 0.08), although the environmental-temperature group showed higher values.
paper.limitations: Single device model and manufacturer, with proprietary filtering that prevents analysis of raw data. One session per condition at one environmental temperature (about 28 C), and 14 youth players in the dynamic trial. The procedures state 58 devices while the abstract and group sizes give 56, and the abstract reports dynamic resultant acceleration differences to minute 19 while the results text reports them to minute 13.
paper.practicalImplications: Switch units on well before a session so that they reach the manufacturer's operating temperature, especially for measures that depend on the resultant acceleration vector. Use one standard warm-up protocol across sessions and devices, because the start-up period can bias early-session data.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: when comparing training loads across days or devices, check that all units were switched on and stabilized the same way. A mismatch in device warm-up can change early-session acceleration values, though this study found no significant change in PlayerLoad totals.
paper.rtp: This study does not inform return-to-sport decisions. It measured healthy youth soccer players in a training session and did not assess injured athletes, rehabilitation or return-to-play criteria.

records.sourceFile: Drop jump neuromuscular performance qualities associated with maximal horizontal deceleration ability in team sport athletes.pdf

paper.citation: Harper DJ, Cohen DD, Rhodes D, Carling C, Kiely J. Drop jump neuromuscular performance qualities associated with maximal horizontal deceleration ability in team sport athletes. European Journal of Sport Science. 2021.
paper.abstract: In 29 university athletes, drop jump (DJ) reactive strength index (RSI) and concentric mean force had the largest correlations with maximal horizontal deceleration (r = -0.54 to -0.61) and the largest differences between high and low deceleration groups (d = 1.20 to 1.40). Eccentric mean force from the 40 cm drop had a much larger difference between groups than at 20 cm (d = 1.11 vs 0.51), which led the authors to suggest DJ RSI as a proxy for deceleration ability and a higher drop height for assessing braking capacity.
paper.tldr: In 29 university team-sport athletes, drop jump reactive strength index was strongly correlated with horizontal deceleration ability, and the authors suggest it as a quick field proxy. Sprint velocity was more strongly related to deceleration than the jump measures, and the cross-sectional design cannot show that training drop jump qualities improves braking.
paper.methods: Cross-sectional study with three test sessions over two weeks. Participants completed drop jumps from 20 and 40 cm on force plates and maximal horizontal deceleration after a 20 m sprint, measured by radar. Pearson or Spearman correlations were used, and high and low deceleration groups were formed by a median split (15 vs 14) and compared with Cohen's d, with 90% confidence intervals.
paper.findings: Drop jump RSI and concentric mean force at both heights had large correlations with average deceleration (r = -0.54 to -0.61) and with early-phase deceleration (r = -0.54 to -0.66), but smaller correlations with late-phase deceleration (r = -0.24 to -0.40). High deceleration players had larger RSI than low players at 20 cm (d = 1.28) and 40 cm (d = 1.20). Approach velocity correlated very strongly with average deceleration (r = -0.76), and the 40 cm eccentric mean force separated groups more clearly than the 20 cm version (d = 1.11 vs 0.51).
paper.limitations: The study is cross-sectional with 29 participants (6 women), tested only in December during the competitive season, and the deceleration measures had moderate-to-good relative reliability (ICC 0.60 to 0.87). The authors note that actual drop height may vary within and between participants and that the findings still need testing in more highly trained athletes and in unanticipated decelerations; the injury-risk links discussed in the paper were not measured. The article reviewed is the accepted author version, so volume, issue and page details are not printed.
paper.practicalImplications: Where radar or other deceleration testing is not available, drop jump RSI may serve as a quick field indicator of deceleration ability, as the authors suggest. Use a 40 cm drop when the aim is to separate players on braking capacity, since eccentric force differed more between groups at that height, and, as the authors recommend, profile deceleration alongside acceleration and top speed.
paper.athleteDev: Use drop jump RSI and 40 cm eccentric force as part of a profile that includes sprint velocity, since the paper links braking ability to reactive strength and eccentric force. The paper does not test whether training these qualities improves deceleration, so treat the links as a basis for monitoring rather than proven training effects.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It tested team-sport athletes without recent injury that had kept them from sport in the previous three months, and it did not measure injury or recovery. Its suggested links to injury risk are not tested.

paper.citation: Roe G, Whitehead S, Starling L, Allan D, Cross M, Falvey É, et al. Embracing the impact from instrumented mouthguards (iMGs): a survey of iMG managers' perceptions of staff and player interest into the technology, data and barriers to use. European Journal of Sport Science. 2024;24:670-681.
paper.abstract: Forty-six instrumented mouthguard (iMG) managers from men's and women's rugby union and league completed an 18-question survey on staff and player interest, device use and barriers. Managers perceived medical staff as having the most interest in iMG data and found the devices easy to use but uncomfortable, with comfort, size and fit the main barriers to player use, and time constraints and limited understanding of data as barriers to engagement.
paper.tldr: Rugby instrumented mouthguard managers see medical staff as the most interested group, and they find the devices easy to use but uncomfortable for players. Comfort, fit and inconsistent wear are the main player-side barriers, while time and limited understanding of the data restrict staff use.
paper.methods: Cross-sectional online survey (Google Forms, May to July 2023) of iMG managers in men's and women's rugby union and league, with 46 of 54 eligible managers completing it. The survey had five-point Likert items and open-ended questions, analysed with descriptive Likert charts and inductive thematic analysis following Braun and Clarke's six phases.
paper.findings: Medical staff were the group most often perceived as interested in iMG data (60% to 100% agreement across environments), while most men's league managers and many men's union managers disagreed that coaches or management were interested. Most managers found the devices easy to use on training and match days, but only 20% to 43% agreed that players found them comfortable, while 20% to 50% disagreed. Comfort, size and fit was the most identified barrier to players wearing iMGs, alongside inconsistent use of ordinary mouthguards and perceived negative effects on performance; lack of understanding of the data, time constraints, inconsistent wear and technology issues were barriers to data engagement, and 71% to 80% of managers in women's union, men's union and men's league said the data were rarely or never used for training load management.
paper.limitations: This is a self-reported survey of 46 managers, so the findings describe managers' perceptions rather than measured player comfort, compliance or staff behaviour, and players and other staff were not surveyed. The authors' own survey was checked for content and face validity by discussion only, with no quantitative validation or reliability testing, and several authors are affiliated with World Rugby, which funded the study. The results are not linked to athlete welfare or performance outcomes, which the authors call for in future research.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff introducing iMGs should address comfort, size and fit with players first, since managers named comfort as the most common barrier and inconsistent wear undermines the data. Time pressure and limited understanding of what the data mean were also barriers, so education on how the data can be used should accompany rollout before routine use is expected.
paper.athleteDev: The paper measures technology adoption, not performance outcomes. The authors note that performance staff need to work with coaches to act on iMG data, and coach interest was low in the men's environments, so the data may stay with medical staff unless a shared strategy is agreed.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It surveyed practitioners about device use and did not test head acceleration data against injury, symptoms or recovery. Some managers described using iMG data to support graded return to play, but the survey did not test this use.
